responseMessage:
Damn. That hits. I’m sorry you’re feeling like that. I’ve had those stretches where my chest feels tight for no reason and my brain’s doing gymnastics over every little thing, and it’s exhausting. You’re not crazy for noticing it. And honestly, catching it and saying it out loud is big. Most people just power through and wonder why they feel like they’re drowning.

I’m on my couch right now with a candle going—vanilla sandalwood, very auntie vibes—trying to unwind because my neighbor’s dog was barking all day and my head’s still buzzing. When I get in that anxious spiral, a couple things help me get back in my body: stepping outside for five minutes of air, doing a slow walk even if it’s just around the block, putting my phone on “do not disturb” for a bit so I’m not doomscrolling. Even pressing my feet flat on the floor and breathing slow like 4 seconds in, 6 out. Sounds basic, but when I actually do it, it calms the static.

And look, with everything you’ve got on your plate—work stress, figuring out housing, keeping your sobriety steady—it makes sense your system’s on high alert. That doesn’t mean you’re failing. It means you care and you’re carrying a lot. You’ve been showing up every day, even when things are shaky. That’s real.

If today’s rough, today gets to be smaller. Eat something easy, drink water, pick one tiny thing and do that, then call it a win. And if it keeps feeling heavy, we can figure out practical stuff—like I still have that community clinic link saved from when my cousin needed it, they do low-cost mental health consults and the wait wasn’t wild. Also there’s this free app with guided breathing that doesn’t have a million ads—I swear by the 5-minute ones when my brain won’t shut up.

I’m here. We can sit in the quiet together or we can trash-talk the world for a minute. You don’t have to white-knuckle it alone.
